splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether actuaries must finalize the assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability before the statutory measurement date or may select them afterward. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing of assumption selection directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled when the supervisee absconds, so the clock stops running and the court retains jurisdiction to revoke supervision after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling the supervised release term when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to extend the term beyond what was specified in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1)—which categorically bars claims previously presented—when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are barred from re-raising any previously presented claim, on top of the separate requirements in § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on previously raised claims in § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a stricter gatekeeping standard.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy the requirements of § 2255(h).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to challenge election rules before an election takes place. The outcome determines whether pre-election challenges to voting procedures are viable, affecting mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office can establish Article III standing to challenge election laws that allegedly dilute or impair the value of lawfully cast votes.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not suffer a sufficiently concrete injury-in-fact from the existence of a ballot-counting deadline law to establish Article III standing for a pre-election challenge.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency interpretations (Auer/Kisor deference) when construing ambiguous provisions of the Sentencing Guidelines that carry criminal consequences.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretation of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. The Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference in the criminal context.

positions.label: Agency deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that when a Sentencing Guideline is genuinely ambiguous, courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's interpretation even when it expands criminal liability, rather than applying the rule of lenity.

positions.label: Lenity trumps agency deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity should take priority over deference to agency interpretations in the criminal context, so ambiguous provisions must be construed in the defendant's favor rather than deferring to the agency's broader reading.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (requiring only one).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision. The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits hold that defendants are disqualified only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits hold that possessing any one of the criteria is disqualifying. The split leads to disparate sentencing outcomes for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on geography.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), giving 'and' its ordinary conjunctive meaning.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' commentary (Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and attempt in the definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses. This split has deepened since Kisor v. Wilkie and affects career-offender sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is entitled to deference as a reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and that conspiracy qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the career-offender provision.

positions.label: Guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) is unambiguous and does not include inchoate offenses, so the commentary impermissibly expands the guideline's scope.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines (U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b)) when the state schedule of controlled substances is broader than the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether state drug convictions involving substances not on the federal schedule can qualify as predicate 'controlled substance offenses' under the career-offender guideline. Some circuits read the guideline broadly to include any state-law drug offense, while others require the substance to also be federally controlled. This affects career-offender determinations and base offense levels.

positions.label: State-schedule-only substances qualify
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law, without requiring the substance to also be controlled under federal law.

positions.label: Substance must also be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a predicate 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under federal law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) may constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as a factor supporting compassionate release. Some circuits categorically bar reliance on such changes, while others allow them as one factor. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement amendment (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) sought to allow such consideration, but some circuits have held the Commission exceeded its authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as one factor, alone or in combination with others, when evaluating whether extraordinary and compelling reasons warrant a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission's contrary policy statement exceeds its statutory authority.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant when revoking supervised release and imposing a revocation sentence, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to sanctioning the breach of trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible purpose of sentences imposed upon revocation of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for their conduct violating supervised release, placing it at 'the extreme of a circuit split,' while other circuits hold that revocation sentences should primarily address the breach of the court's trust rather than serve a punitive function.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, treating the revocation sentence as a punitive measure for the violating conduct.

positions.label: Revocation is about breach of trust, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should primarily sanction the defendant's breach of the court's trust in granting supervised release, rather than serve as punishment for the underlying violating conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees filed in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but acknowledged the existence of a circuit split.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the terms (but not necessarily the fact or duration) of imprisonment must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring civil rights claims.
splits.description: Circuits have been split for decades on whether challenges to conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions (such as denials of prerelease custody transfers under the First Step Act) must be brought as habeas petitions or may proceed as civil rights actions. The Supreme Court has repeatedly noted but not resolved this question, leaving an entrenched circuit split.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges BOP decisions affecting the duration or execution of confinement, habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy, precluding civil rights claims.

positions.label: Civil rights claims also available
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions may proceed via civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens) even when habeas might also be available.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted in good faith to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate, while the dissent noted this creates a circuit split with circuits reading § 348(f)(1)(A) to protect debtors' post-petition equity gains.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity are property of the estate upon conversion to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects good-faith converting debtors by excluding post-petition appreciation from the converted estate, preserving equity gains for the debtor.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order,' while other circuits have generally not recognized such orders as immediately appealable. The D.C. Circuit acknowledged that the First Circuit similarly views medical privacy as strong but that circuit practice varies.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that cannot be adequately vindicated by later appeal.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are generally not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine, as the interest can be adequately protected through other procedural mechanisms.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether claims that could also be raised in a § 2255 habeas petition—such as claims of legal error in the conviction or sentence—may be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. Some circuits allow such consideration, while others hold that compassionate release cannot serve as a substitute for habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's underlying conviction or sentence as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an appropriate vehicle for relitigating claims that belong in a § 2255 motion, and such errors cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether duplicate electronic images of child pornography count as distinct images for purposes of the sentencing enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 2G2.2(b)(7)(D).
splits.description: Courts disagree on whether duplicated copies of the same child pornography image should be counted individually or only once when calculating the number of images for sentencing enhancement purposes. The Fifth Circuit held that duplicates count as distinct images, deepening a split on how to tally images across devices and file systems.

positions.label: Duplicates count as distinct images
positions.summary: Holds that each copy of an image, including exact duplicates, counts as a separate image for sentencing enhancement purposes under the child pornography Guidelines.

positions.label: Duplicates should not be double-counted
positions.summary: Holds that duplicate copies of the same image should be counted only once for sentencing purposes, focusing on unique images rather than total file count.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
